episodes.text: At around age 5, during a nationalist boycott-of-foreign-goods campaign, deliberately burned her own cherished English-made doll -- a self-initiated demonstration of nationalist commitment, not merely one imposed by her parents.

At age 12, after being denied formal Congress party membership for being underage, took on and actually ran the "Vanar Sena," a children's brigade doing real underground logistics work for the freedom movement -- the organizational idea originated with her mother and a Congress official who selected her as leader, but she was the one who ran it in practice.

Grew up with chronic parental absence -- her mother frequently and seriously ill (dying of tuberculosis when Indira was 18-19), her father repeatedly imprisoned for long stretches -- leaving her effectively without either parent present for extended periods through childhood and adolescence.

Endured direct emotional wounds in childhood/adolescence (an aunt calling her "ugly and stupid" around age 14; her father's dismissive response to her expressed teenage depression); as an adult, in a 1958 verse in her own words, described her own thoughts as flying "like bats in ghostly confusion" -- self-described restless, anxious inner mental activity, not just a biographer's characterization.

Her marriage to Feroze Gandhi deteriorated over years (his multiple affairs, her own one affair, her father's active pressure on Feroze to remain married rather than separate); Feroze responded in part by publicly, passive-aggressively criticizing her father's government from his own seat in Parliament.

As Congress Party President (1959), helped engineer the dismissal of a democratically elected communist-led state government in Kerala -- an early instance of willingness to use central/party authority against a state government she opposed politically.

Selected for the premiership in 1966 by senior Congress power-brokers specifically because they expected her to be a controllable, "pliable cipher" figurehead ("gungi gudiya"/dumb doll); within a few years, contrary to that expectation, moved to consolidate personal power and systematically removed the senior figures who had elevated her.

In 1969, pushed through nationalization of 14 major commercial banks (holding roughly 85% of national deposits) by ordinance over fierce internal party opposition, making her own Finance Minister's position untenable; when he declined a consolation post and resigned, the party split and expelled her, and she retained the majority of sitting MPs in the resulting split.

During the 1971 crisis with Pakistan, despite strong domestic pressure for immediate military intervention amid a refugee crisis, deliberately delayed direct military action for months, warning Parliament in her own words that "a wrong step... would have an effect different from the desired one" -- reasoning that premature action would let Pakistan frame the conflict as an Indian-manufactured conspiracy.

After Kissinger told her directly the US would not help India against China while concealing his own imminent secret trip to China routed through Pakistan, responded to the dual US/China pressure by reversing an earlier position and concluding the Indo-Soviet security treaty she had previously rejected in 1969, negotiated by her aides "with urgency and in total secrecy."

Undertook a personal diplomatic tour of the Soviet Union, Western Europe, and the US ahead of the 1971 war, meeting Nixon directly in Washington and holding her ground on India's independent position despite the US's clear tilt toward Pakistan.

When her Army Chief advised that launching operations during the monsoon season was militarily inadvisable and recommended waiting for winter, she accepted his professional judgment and adjusted the campaign timeline accordingly, despite intense political pressure for immediate action.

When the Allahabad High Court voided her own 1971 election for "dishonest election practices" and barred her from office for six years, rejected calls -- including from within her own party -- to resign, and appealed instead.

Days after the Supreme Court granted only a conditional stay of the adverse verdict, personally drove to the President's residence at night to present her already-made decision to declare a national Emergency, informing even her own inner circle only afterward, as a fait accompli.

Announced the Emergency herself, direct to the nation via a late-night radio broadcast, publicly framing the move as a defensive response to a conspiracy against her reform agenda rather than as a response to the adverse court verdict against her personally.

During the 21-month Emergency, presided over mass arrests (roughly 110,000 people), press censorship described as among the most stringent in Indian history, and did not curb the forced-sterilization campaign (millions sterilized, with documented deaths from botched procedures) or associated mass displacement while they were ongoing, holding ultimate political authority throughout.

Is documented as having "doted blindly" on her son Sanjay, who held no official government position, and enabled rather than checked his exercise of extra-constitutional authority (media/film censorship, expelling foreign journalists, pressuring celebrities) during the Emergency, to the point that his informal power base reportedly out-governed the official Prime Minister's Office.
Stated her own instrumental view of democracy during the Emergency period: "Democracy is not an end. It is merely a system by which one proceeds towards the goal."

In January 1977, unexpectedly ended the Emergency and called fresh elections despite not being externally compelled to do so and being able to plausibly continue indefinitely; the subsequent election was judged largely free and fair, she lost decisively including her own seat, and she accepted the defeat, transferring power peacefully.

After being arrested in October 1977 on corruption-related charges and released unconditionally the next day on procedural grounds, publicly reframed the arrest as political persecution intended "to prevent" her "from going to the people" -- a framing that reportedly gained her public sympathy rather than damaging her further.

Roughly 18 months after her 1977 electoral defeat, won a parliamentary by-election and returned to Parliament from the opposition benches -- an active political comeback rather than withdrawal from public life -- and by January 1980 her party won a landslide return to full power.

After her son Sanjay's sudden death in a plane crash (1980) -- a period multiple sources tie to greater insecurity and instability in her decision-making -- actively persuaded her previously reluctant elder son Rajiv, a commercial airline pilot with no political ambitions, to enter politics in Sanjay's place.

Her party had reportedly initially supported the rise of a militant Sikh preacher in Punjab in the 1970s as a strategy to split and weaken a rival regional party's political base; he subsequently broke from any such control and led an armed separatist campaign, escalating to armed occupation of Sikhism's holiest site by 1983.

After the breakdown of negotiations and her rejection of a proposed political settlement, ordered the Indian Army to storm the occupied Golden Temple complex (Operation Blue Star, June 1984), resulting in hundreds of deaths and destruction of major religious structures -- later widely characterized, including by her own political successors, as a costly mistake she ultimately "paid for with her life."

The day before her assassination, delivered a public speech stating "I may not be here tomorrow" and recounting a long history of physical attacks against her, concluding "I do not care whether I live or die" -- a documented public statement made in apparent awareness of ongoing danger; she is also reported to have written funeral instructions in the period before her death, in apparent anticipation of her own assassination.
